clue.text: 'Old boiler' — is that PC?

definitions.meaning: an old-fashioned metal tub heated to boil laundry, once found in every British wash-house
a police constable, for whom this metal is old slang

explanation.surface: A sneer at someone called an old boiler, followed by the question of whether the phrase is politically correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PC' looks like 'politically correct' after the insult, but it means police constable. An 'old boiler' is British slang for an unattractive older woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: a laundry boiler made of that metal, and British slang for a policeman.

clue.text: Sort of state feared most by those old Tories who . had one?

definitions.text: Sort of state feared most by those old Tories who . had one?

parts.words: Sort of state feared most by those old Tories who . had one?
parts.note: the '... state' is the Tory jibe at interfering government, while the upper-class Tories were themselves brought up by a children's nurse

explanation.surface: A dig at old Tories who hate interfering government yet were raised by hired help.
explanation.walkthrough: The irony: the same word names the overprotective state Tories decry and the nursemaid who reared them.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's nurse employed by a family, and also the label in 'nanny state' for paternalistic government.

clue.text: One sort of HRT gets one cross, making you a beastly killer

parts.note: one is AN, the indefinite article

indicators.note: a sort of HRT is a reworked version of those three letters

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article again
a cross is the letter X

explanation.surface: Hormone replacement therapy picks up an unexpected side effect and becomes lethal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' gives AN and the second 'one' gives A: both forms of the indefinite article count as one. 'sort of' is the anagram signal on HRT.
explanation.definitionFit: The disease is a bacterial infection of cattle and sheep that can kill both animals and people.

clue.text: Ghastly hotelier, capital lost, at rock bottom, wanted for fraud

indicators.note: the capital, or first letter, of the name is dropped

parts.note: Basil Fawlty, the appalling hotel owner in the British sitcom Fawlty Towers
the lowest point is the nadir

explanation.surface: A dreadful hotel owner, broke and at his lowest, is sought by police for fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: Basil Fawlty is the hotelier of the British sitcom Fawlty Towers. The tycoon behind Polly Peck fled Britain in 1993 to escape fraud charges.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polly Peck businessman jumped bail for northern Cyprus while facing theft and fraud charges in Britain.

clue.text: See 21
Women have been controversially turning on dear Di

definitions.note: the definition is a sentence missing its final word: women made priests, a disputed change

indicators.note: turning signals that the letters of the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Women have been fiercely attacking Princess Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a sentence with a blank: women have been controversially made priests, as the Church of England did in 1994. 'turning on' looks like 'attacking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Admitted to holy orders, which the Church of England first did for women priests in 1994, amid fierce dispute.

clue.text: See 12
Architect of local government scandal

parts.note: John ... was a Yorkshire architect whose bribery of councillors became a major 1970s corruption affair

explanation.surface: A plain description of the man who masterminded a council corruption affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Architect' reads as 'mastermind', but he was literally an architect, jailed in 1974 for bribing officials.
explanation.definitionFit: John Poulson, a real architect, was the central figure of the 1970s bribery scandal in British councils.

clue.text: Brit abroad of ever diminishing service to the world?

definitions.text: of ever diminishing service to the world?

indicators.note: abroad means all over the place, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A Briton overseas who is less and less use to the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' rearranges BRIT. John Birt, BBC Director-General in the 1990s, was blamed for cuts to the BBC World Service.
explanation.definitionFit: John Birt ran the BBC while its World Service was cut back, so he was of diminishing service to the world.

clue.text: What Thatcher said she'd never do: inject money to achieve recovery

indicators.note: inject means put inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.words: What Thatcher said she'd never do
parts.note: Margaret Thatcher declared 'The lady's not for turning', ruling out a reversal of policy
P is penny, small money

explanation.surface: Pumping money into the economy for a recovery, the very reversal Thatcher swore she'd never make.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher's 1980 line 'The lady's not for turning' refused any U-turn; 'inject' puts P inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An improvement or rise, as in an economic upswing after a slump.

clue.text: Can hurt expression be concealed by maligned Hallo!? Yes

indicators.note: concealed by means held inside the other piece
maligned means badly treated, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: ow is a cry of pain
Y stands for yes, as on Y/N forms

explanation.surface: Can a hurt cry hide behind a mocked greeting? Apparently so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' is the definition, not a verb: slang for prison, here the London women's jail. 'maligned' is the anagram signal and 'concealed by' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Holloway was London's best-known women's prison, and 'can' is slang for a jail.

clue.text: A paper tiger to opponents and supporters alike

definitions.text: A paper tiger to opponents and supporters alike

parts.words: A paper tiger to opponents and supporters alike
parts.note: the newspaper industry's own ... watchdog, mocked as toothless by critics and backers alike

explanation.surface: A description of something fierce-looking but powerless, as both its enemies and friends agree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper tiger' means a toothless threat, and here it is literally a tiger about papers: the body that policed British newspapers from 1991 to 2014.
explanation.definitionFit: The self-regulating newspaper watchdog was widely seen as having no teeth, so it was a paper tiger in both senses.

clue.text: His bloody features are shocking, his players all swear

definitions.text: His bloody features are shocking, his players all swear

parts.words: His bloody features are shocking, his players all swear
parts.note: Quentin ... films are known for graphic violence and characters who curse constantly

explanation.surface: A complaint about a man whose face is gory and whose team members curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'features' means feature films, not a face, and 'players' are actors; 'bloody' works as both gory and a swear word.
explanation.definitionFit: The film director of Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction is famous for violent scenes and profane dialogue.

clue.text: Journalist sap swallows Duchess's opening: 'It's not been tried yet'

parts.note: a sub, or sub-editor, is a newspaper journalist

indicators.note: swallows means takes inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: sap is plant juice

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A reporter hints that the Duchess's latest revelation hasn't faced trial yet.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'sub' is a sub-editor, a newspaper journalist who checks copy. 'swallows' is the container and 'opening' picks the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin legal phrase for a case still before the court and not yet decided, so reporting on it is restricted.

clue.text: For today's players, perhaps, it takes a bit of poetry to get high

parts.note: a line is a single row of verse
up means high or raised

explanation.surface: A remark that modern performers need some verse to get stoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'players' are a sports team; 'perhaps' marks today's team sheet as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The team selected to play on a given day is the team list, an ordered roster of names.

clue.text: Nothing in Chunnel moving due to blow-out

indicators.note: in means placed inside the other piece
moving means the letters shift around

parts.note: nothing is the letter O, as zero

explanation.surface: Nothing is moving in the Channel Tunnel because of a tyre burst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges CHUNNEL and 'in' puts O within it. 'blow-out' means a big feast, not a burst tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A blow-out is slang for a lavish meal, and this word is a formal midday meal.

clue.text: Fat arse vital to some old banger?

parts.note: fat means big
the end is the rear or backside

explanation.surface: A large backside that matters in an old sausage, or perhaps an old car.
explanation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for both a sausage and an old car; the engine part is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: In a piston engine it is the connecting-rod bearing on the crankshaft, essential to an old car.

clue.text: No longer getting sex by credit card? Here's a way out

parts.note: ex means former, no longer so
it is slang for sex
Visa is a credit card brand

explanation.surface: A former lover now paying for sex with plastic offers an escape.
explanation.definitionFit: A permit to leave a country, so a document providing an exit.

clue.text: Cries of 'Socialist leader puts it on thick!'

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: creams means spreads cream on, applying it thickly

explanation.surface: A socialist leader is accused of laying it on thick and exaggerating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts it on thick' suggests exaggeration but here means applying cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud, shrill shouts or howls; also slang for very funny things.

clue.text: Sex with Kennedy — something royal watchers flaunt?

parts.note: union is sexual union
Jack was the nickname of President John F Kennedy

explanation.surface: A JFK sex scandal, the sort of thing royal-watching gossip thrives on.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal fans line the route waving the British flag.

clue.text: Faldo no Atherton at heart, being bound to respond honestly

indicators.note: at heart signals letters lying within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Golfer Nick Faldo is no Mike Atherton, the England cricket captain, deep down, being bound to answer honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Faldo was a British golfer and Mike Atherton England's cricket captain; 'at heart' picks letters from inside their names.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sworn to tell the truth, as a witness is in court.

clue.text: Insulting to the finish, it's said, this MP

definitions.text: Insulting to the finish, it's said, this MP

parts.words: Insulting to the finish, it's said, this MP
parts.note: the London Labour MP was criticised in 1996 for remarks about blonde Finnish nurses, and finish sounds like Finnish

explanation.surface: An MP who keeps up the insults right to the end, so people report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the finish' seems to mean 'to the end', but read with 'it's said' it is 'to the Finnish': the Hackney MP was attacked in 1996 for disparaging Finnish nurses.
explanation.definitionFit: The Labour MP for Hackney North caused a stir in 1996 with comments on Finnish nurses in her local hospital.

clue.text: Brenda's people ain't no different!

definitions.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose people are her subjects

indicators.note: different means the letters are made different, rearranged

explanation.surface: A cockney insists the Queen's subjects are just the same as everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brenda' is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's subjects make up the country's population, its people as a whole.

clue.text: Retreat after second-rate leader

indicators.note: after means the retreat word comes behind the grade letter

parts.note: B is a second-class grade
a lair is an animal's retreat or den

explanation.surface: A politician retreats in the wake of a mediocre leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Blair became Labour Party leader in 1994.

clue.text: Richard's wrinkly organ

parts.note: Richard Ingrams founded a magazine for older readers in 1992, and organ means a publication

explanation.surface: A smutty reference to an elderly man's body part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' means a publication and 'wrinkly' an older person: Richard Ingrams, ex-editor of Private Eye, founded the magazine for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Ingrams' magazine is aimed at older readers, a journal for wrinklies.

clue.text: Live broadcast — Conservative has no alternative but flippancy

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered, so the letters are spread out anew
has no means the following piece is removed

parts.note: a Tory is a Conservative
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: On live broadcast, a Conservative has nothing left but jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' turns LIVE into LEVI; 'has no' takes OR out of TORY, leaving TY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lightness of manner, a lack of due seriousness, as with frivolity.

clue.text: Labour leader's bottom

definitions.meaning: Michael ... led the Labour Party from 1980 to 1983
the lowest part, as of a page or mountain

explanation.surface: A rude comment about a Labour leader's backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Foot led Labour; the word also means the base or lowest part of something.

clue.text: See 12
